#2107. Kevin De Bruyne to leave Napoli 'the sooner the better', his wife announces: Man City legend, 35, desperate to quit his 'not nice existence' after rows with team-mates, bosses and fan issues

Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:58 EST, 13 November 2026

Kevin De Bruyne's wife Michelle has opened up on her family's struggles in Naples and desire to move back home to Belgium one day.

De Bruyne, 35, joined Napoli in the summer of 2025 after leaving Manchester City following a legendary ten-year spell.

But things haven't gone to plan in Italy, with De Bruyne struggling for fitness in his first season, while he also clashed with former boss Antonio Conte.

The situation hasn't improved much this time around under Max Allegri as Napoli currently sit 10th in Serie A, and reports broke earlier this season that the Belgian midfielder was involved in a dressing room bust-up with team-mates.

And De Bruyne's wife Michele, who he married in 2017, reflected on the turbulence in an interview with Belgian magazine NINA back in September.

'Of course, we think about the future together,' he said. 'And increasingly often, we say to each other: "We are going to live here in Limburg. The sooner we get here, the better".'

Kevin De Bruyne's wife Michelle has opened up on her family's struggles living in Naples

De Bruyne moved to Napoli in the summer of 2025 after a glittering 10 years at Manchester City

Limburg is a province in Belgium, and although Michelle insisted that she thought Naples was a beautiful place to live with great weather and food, she spoke about the toll that life in Italy has had on her partner and their three children, Mason, Rome and Suri.

'Kevin leads a very restricted life in Napoli,' she added. 'It's not much fun for him. Besides, we can't do anything together as a family in the city. That's the other side of the coin, isn't it?

'In Manchester, it was different. Where we lived, people had seen us so often that it wasn’t special anymore. We could walk out the door there without a single photo being taken. In Naples, that is impossible.'

She later added: 'At a certain point, football is no longer the priority. You have achieved everything, done everything. Why would you then turn your children’s lives upside down?'

De Bruyne, who is one of the highest paid players in Italy, signed a two-year contract when he arrived at Napoli but it wasn't certain that he would make it into the second part of that deal in the summer.

Reflecting on his first year ahead of the World Cup, De Bruyne insisted he was 'happy' that Conte had departed.

'Obviously it was difficult for me because Conte has a very different vision of football to mine,' De Bruyne said.

'In truth, I never had the opportunity to play in my preferred position. In any case, I always tried to give my all for the team. We played very defensively. If you try to win every game by a one-goal margin with a 4-5-1 formation, you play a certain type of football.

De Bruyne signed a two-year deal at Napoli and is unlikely to extend his time in Italy

'At the start of the season, we sat back even deeper. Our centre-forward scored just 10 goals, so you know the statistics are not going to be great…'

He later added: 'For me, yes (I'm happy Conte has gone). As far as I am concerned, he was not obliged to stay. There were promises made last summer on the way that we would be playing, but at the end of the day not much of it happened.

'I found that a pity. Football needs to be enjoyable, and unfortunately, I found that aspect lacking.

'There’s no point beating around the bush, we have different visions of football. I never got to play in my position under Conte.'

#2106. Millwall controversy takes fresh twist - West Ham will be watching on

A fresh twist has emerged concerning the off-pitch drama at Millwall involving once highly-rated winger, Benicio Baker-Boaitey.

The Lions' start to the Championship season has been one of mixed fortunes, with Alex Neil's side sat 16th, having accumulated 18 points 15 matches.

Neil, one of the second tier's most seasoned managers, has been without several key names so far this season due to injury and suspension issues, which hasn't helped his side's wish for consistency.

One of the players missing in action for quite some time now is Baker-Boaitey, with it initially envisaged that the 22-year-old was also on the treatment table for a prolonged period.

However, recent developments have shed new light on the winger's situation, and it is one which could be about to get worse.

Baker-Boaitey arrived at Millwall in January 2025 after a spell with Premier League outfit, Brighton and Hove Albion, where he made six top-flight appearances for the Seagulls under Roberto De Zerbi after debuting against Chelsea in December 2023.

He would then link up with Port Vale for the 2024/25 League Two season, before his gametime in North Staffordshire was cut short due to injury, with Neil admitting after his move to SE16 was completed that Baker-Boaitey was suffering with pubic symphysis.

Almost two years later, though, the winger is yet to make a first-team appearance for the Lions, and was recently seen posting cryptic Instagram posts, one of which was captioned: "On my mumma, can't even train with the 21s."

His account has since been deactivated, and it has since been widely reported that Millwall are now undertaking disciplinary action, which could even result in the termination of his contract, whilst Baker-Boaitey is also said to be weighing up his options.

Given Brighton's recent ability for producing and unearthing several gems, there was an understandable hype when Millwall added Baker-Boaitey to their squad so soon after the club-record sale of Romain Esse - who has since returned to the club on loan - to Crystal Palace.

“Another England youth international, Benicio ticks a number of boxes we’re looking to recruit for at his young age of 21," said Lions director of football, Steve Gallen.

"He is an exciting winger who will add plenty of pace and skill to the squad, which will get fans off their seats."

However, this prediction has failed to come true, with Baker-Boaitey only making one appearance for the club's Under-21s side shortly after moving from the AMEX Stadium.

Millwall and West Ham United fans' disdain towards one another is certainly well-documented, and was displayed at The Den two months ago in a compelling 2-2 draw.

However, those from East London will certainly have one eye on how their rivals' disciplinary investigation into Baker-Boaitey's conduct plays out.

Indeed, the former England youth international came through the famous academy at Rush Green, and by 2020, aged 16, was linked with a move to Bayern Munich after rejecting professional terms at the London Stadium, eventually signing for FC Porto, with West Ham receiving £190,000 in compensation.

Millwall and West Ham fans, what do you make of the saga involving Benicio Baker-Boaitey? Comment below!

The German giants were not alone when it came to high-profile clubs courting his signature, with the likes of Liverpool, Paris Saint-Germain and Manchester United also credited with interest.

Since Baker-Boaitey's social media swipe, Neil is yet to issue a statement on the matter, and neither has the player.

Millwall will be hoping that this doesn't cause any form of distraction regardless of Baker-Boaitey's distinct lack of involvement since joining the club, whilst further impressions could be made on West Ham fans, even if returning to form under new head coach, Scott Parker, is their top focus right now.

At present, Milan are in a good place. Although they’ve had a few disappointing results in midweek games, they’ve largely been solid when it’s mattered and picked up several really impressive results.

For Cardinale, it’s been a great start to life under Ruben Amorim – who he backed heavily in the summer – and the hope is that it will continue for the foreseeable future. In January, more investments are planned, and the aim is to continue the upward trajectory.

#2104. Swansea City backed for Roberto Martinez or Pablo Hernandez move

Swansea City have had to take a double-hit in recent weeks, with a dip in form and interest in their manager from elsewhere, but FLW's Swans fan pundit is optimistic over the identity of his replacement.

Swansea City's ascent to the top of the Championship was one of the surprises of the start of the season in the second tier. Seven wins from their first ten games took them to the top of the pile, while other below them struggled to find the consistency required to dislodge them.

That, however, all came to a juddering stop in the month building up to the international break. Four defeats in their last five have dropped them to sixth place in the table, and there was more bad news for them with reports that head coach Vitor Matos is in the sights of Ligue Un club Strasbourg.

With Matos's departure for France imminent, Swansea are in the hunt for a new manager, and with the top half of the Championship table looking extremely tight this season and tricky matches coming up, whoever the new incumbent is will need to get the team back on form to build on their excellent start.

Football League World have been in contact with our Swans fan pundit Will Hughes about the changing of the guard at The Swansea.com Stadium, and in particular about the possibility of the former West Bromwich Albion manager Carlos Corberan coming to his club, and Will believes that his club currently enticing enough to attract that calibre of manager: "I think Corberan would be good. He's certainly a name that should be floating around there."

Will believes that his club is a more attractive option as a result of changes behind the scenes over the last couple of years: "Honestly, I don't know who Matos's replacement is going to be. I'm not sure how big our pull is now, but I'd definitely say that the Swans job is a lot more desirable now managers now than what it was this time last year, for where we are in the league, the outside noise with over goings-on at the club, with the ownership of Modric and Snoop Dogg, and the fact that we've got more finance now. We've got a better squad. It's definitely a more desirable club."

Will is setting his hopes high over the identity of the next Swansea boss, with one former manager being someone he'd love to see back at his club: "This time last year I certainly wouldn't have been saying some of the names that are floating about now. One name that's been floated by Swans fans has been Roberto Martinez. I would love it if he came home, but dare I say maybe he's a bit above us after managing Portugal and Belgium, two very high profile jobs. Would he see this as a step down? Maybe he doesn't want to ruin his legacy here. I can't see it happening, but I'd love it."

And he had another suggestion with a Swansea connection who he feels could be a realistic target for his club: "Pablo Hernandez has been noted. Castellon are in the same bracket as us under Jamestown Analytics, Tony Bloom's company. I don't know whether they have a clause that we can't import another Jamestown club's manager, but going by the outside noise and the statistics that we see from Castellon, he could be a good fit for us."

Will sees the replacement as potentially an opportunity for his club, and is grateful to Matos for his role in improving Swansea's profile: "I don't whether we'd be looking higher. For me, I'd love it if we upgraded on Matos. Matos came in and he did his job. When he came in, Swans were floundering near the bottom. He kept us up and got us to a mid-table finish, which is what we were expecting, and now this year we've had a really good start, he's got us in the play-offs, near the top of the division. Whether he'd have kept us there we'll never know, but he got us to that point so he deserves credit for making the job more desirable."

Who would you like to see as the new Swansea City manager? Let us know in the comments below!

Our Swansea correspondent is also aware of the importance of the new manager stepping straight in and getting the team back on track: "So the question is can we get someone to keep us there or maybe take us a little bit further up. You'd want someone who's going to come in and hit the ground running. I know it's not as easy as that, but you don't want to bring in someone where you're thinking, "Maybe it'll work, maybe it won't." You want to upgrade. I don't know how far our pull is now, with Jamestown on board, whether we can look at the bigger leagues, at clubs and managers we wouldn't have over the last few years. There's a few out of work. You've mentioned Corberan, I've mentioned Roberto Hernandez. Kieran McKenna would be good, but I've heard we're priced out on him."

And he has one particular fixture in mind, which is coming up on the 29th November: "It's typical that the new manager's first game is probably going to be the South Wales derby. Hopefully it'll be another Garry Monk masterclass; 3-0 in his first game. But we'd hope it doesn't go the way it did afterwards towards the end of his tenure, because it turned sour in the end. I keep saying we'll wait and see. I'd an expect an announcement today that Matos has gone, but we've got Leon Brittan and Chris O'Leary, two legends, looking after us for two games and you'd think hopefully we'll get a new manager in next week, and we can go from there."

Will feels that while the Cardiff game is extremely important, Swansea's season won't be defined by his team's matches against these opponents: "All I would say to Swans fans is not to get on the new manager's back if we don't get the result we want against Cardiff. As much as we all want to beat them, it's a marathon not a sprint. We may lose to them but beat them away from home. Let's not jump on the new manager's back, or Leon Brittan or the club if we don't win that game. It's not the end of the world. It may feel like it, believe me. I've got into some stinking moods when we've lost to Cardiff in the past."

And he believes that the best thing that his fellow supporters can do is get fully behind the team, no matter who the opponents: "But whoever's in charge, let's not get on their back. It was different when we had someone like Michael Duff or Luke Williams when they lost their last South Wales derbies because of the situations that were going on, Luke Williams flirting with West Brom and Michael Duff saying what he said about the derby, so that's fair enough. But let's not get on their back, let's get behind them and hopefully start with a win on Saturday. It's a tricky game against West Brom, but forget about the fact that we haven't got a manager or where they are in the league, it's a game we've got to try and win to stop the rot of our poor form."

Whoever it is who ends up filling the shoes of Vitor Matos at The Swansea.com Stadium will have one immediate job; to turn around the form of a team who were flying at the start of the season. Given that Swansea City haven't finished above 10th place in the Championship in the previous five years, few were expecting them to get near the top of the table this time around, but they managed this on the 1st September and stayed there for most of the next six weeks.

The names mentioned in connection with the vacant position all have something to recommend them. Carlos Corberan has Championship experience from spells with Huddersfield Town and West Bromwich Albion. Pablo Hernandez has a previous Swansea connection from having played there from 2012 to 2014. And Kieran McKenna built a strong reputation from taking Ipswich Town from League One to the Premier League.

And whoever the identity of the new Swansea manager might be, he'll have a tough start. West Bromwich Albion are the Swans' next opponents, and they're one place above them in the table. Next after that come Middlesbrough, who are in second place in the table. And then comes the big derby game against Cardiff City.

So the question facing the club is that of which was the blip? Were Swansea City just on an explosively good run of form at the start of the season which is now settling towards where most people would have put them in the summer, or did Vitor Matos build a squad that is capable of going the entire gruelling length of a 46-game season near the top of the table?

Whichever the answer to that question turns out to be, what is undeniable is that Swansea City demonstrated their potential over the opening two months of the season. If the new Swansea manager can capture that form again, the Swans could yet find themselves pushing to end their nine-year exile in the Championship by its end.

#2103. Why must Manchester United move beyond the Glazers?

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

The Glazers took control of Manchester United in 2005. That takeover has since caused so many disruptions and protests by the fans over massive debts and insufficient backing of the team in the transfer market, despite successful periods in the Premier League and Europe.

Now Manchester United need to think about who should control the club in the future. Laurie Whitwell has now shared his views on why Manchester United need an ownership change. He simply wants the Glazers gone from Old Trafford. However, he also recognizes that replacing the current ownership doesn’t automatically mean things will improve for United.

The journalist believes the change in ownership has had a lasting effect on United, with the club still feeling its consequences today. A fresh start might be welcome, but the identity of the next owners would matter just as much as the departure of the existing ones.

“Personally, I would like to see the Glazers gone from Manchester United,” Laurie Whitwell said on The Rest is Football podcast with Gary Lineker.

“That change, you know, just really affected and still impacts United now.”

The desire for different ownership is one thing, but finding people capable of taking the club forward is another.

Whitwell admitted there is no perfect answer when it comes to who should take charge.

That leaves United facing a difficult choice. A sale could offer the chance to change how the club is run, but simply bringing in a new owner would not guarantee better decisions or a brighter future.

Whitwell also raised the idea of United supporters having a greater say in the club’s ownership and decisions, much like the Barcelona model where fans own the club itself. However, he highlighted that the Barcelona model isn’t ideal either and has its own shortcomings.

Changing the names at the top would only be one part of the change. The club would also need an ownership structure capable of making sound decisions and providing a direction.

The issue of ownership goes beyond whether the Glazers should stay or leave. Manchester United needs to find the right people and the right model to secure the club’s future. Getting that decision wrong could leave them facing the same circus the fans are enduring under the Glazers.

#2102. The EFL Championship's top 9 wealthiest owners in 2026/27

The 2026-27 Championship is firmly underway and it's as intriguing as ever.

And with two more play-off spots opening up for the 2026-27 season, the chase for the Premier League riches is more hotly-contested than ever in the second tier of English football.

New financial measures are also coming into place, with profit & sustainability rules (PSR) being taken away and incoming are squad cost rules (SCR), where owners can only invest £33 million in equity over a three-year period, whilst player and manager costs can only amount to 85 per cent of a club's yearly turnover.

Owners tend to need deep pockets to fund a promotion-chasing club in the Championship - but who are the nine wealthiest owners in the second tier ahead of next season? FLW takes a look...

For the longest time, Norwich City were ran by celebrity chef Delia Smith and her husband Michael Wynn-Jones, having joined the club's board in 1996 before becoming majority shareholders in 1998.

Seeking outside investment though for someone with far deeper pockets than themselves, enter Mark Attanasio, who after initially being appointed as a director at Carrow Road in 2022, became the majority shareholder in 2024 - much like how Smith and Wynn-Jones came to being in control 26 years prior.

With prior experience and ownership at Baseball side the Milwaukee Brewers, Attanasio was seen as an ideal fit to take Norwich to the next level, and he now owns 85 per cent of the Norfolk outfit - with a net worth of $1.9 billion (£1.4 billion), according to Forbes, the 68-year-old certainly has the cash to try and take them back to the Premier League.

Blackburn Rovers are into their 16th year of the Venky's ownership, and to say it's been turbulent would be an understatement.

The glory days of Jack Walker's ownership had long gone when the Indian poultry giants purchased the Lancashire outfit from Walker's trust in 2010, but under their guidance, relegation from the Premier League came in 2012 - and they've never returned.

Despite the Rao family not attending a match since January 2013, they still continue to fund the club's annual losses, even if in recent times there has been struggles getting money out of their native India and to the UK, but they have a lot of finance, and as per a report from The News in 2025, the Venky's were worth an estimated £1.56 billion.

With restrictions from the High Court of Delhi now lifted ahead of 2026-27, could the Venky's be ready to invest more into the club's squad to guide them away from another potential relegation battle? Only time will tell...

The Coates family have been involved in Stoke City since 1986, when Peter Coates became majority shareholder and chairman, but after selling to an Icelandic consortium in 1999, he would return seven years later, and in 2015, his son John would become vice-chairman.

Coates junior has worked his way up the ranks since, and in 2024, a change to the ownership structure saw John become sole owner of the club, and he is the one pulling the strings and making the big decisions on who comes and goes at the bet365 Stadium.

Bet365 has been a big business win for the Coates family, and as per Forbes' real-time net worth analysis, Coates himself is worth an estimated £2.3 billion, and despite Stoke's stagnation in the Championship recently, there's seemingly no sign of the funding stopping at the Staffordshire club.

QPR have had turbulent ownership changes over the years, with the eras of Flavio Briatore and Bernie Ecclestone, then Tony Fernandes well and truly in the past.

The current ownership group at Loftus Road is mainly led by Malaysian businessman Ruben Gnanalingam, who owns just under 60 per cent of the Hoops, US investor Richard Reilly holds 21 per cent and former chairman Amit Bhatia also holding 20 per cent.

Whilst Gnanalingam's personal wealth isn't known, the family wealth sits at a healthy £2.3 billion, as per Forbes, with much of their successful business coming from the shipping industry in the form of Westports Holdings.

Gnanalingam is the executive chairman and group managing director of the company, with the 49-year-old being a part of the furniture in the QPR hierarchy since the Fernandes days in 2011 - that doesn't look set to change anytime soon, and with signings recently such as Richard Kone and Ronnie Edwards, he's definitely been putting his money where his mouth is.

From the outside looking in, it may represent something of a surprise that, in Steve Lansdown, Bristol City have the fifth-richest owner at Championship level.

The Bristolian has held his position as chairman of the Robins since 2002, and is the founder of Bristol Sport alongside coupling his duties at Ashton Gate with a majority shareholder role with both Bristol Bears and Bristol Flyers.

This means that, as per Forbes, Lansdown's net worth sits at a whopping £2.38 billion. However, in contrast to other counterparts both on this list and outside of it, the 73-year-old's personal wealth has hardly been translated into a healthy transfer warchest for the Robins to utilise over the years.

Lansdown has undertaken serious work away from the field to help Bristol City grow, such as the impressive £40 million redevelopment of Ashton Gate around a decade ago, although his lack of investment into the playing squad has been a frequent point of frustration for supporters.

The Robins have significant potential and all the foundations are in place for that to be achieved, bar one - you do get the impression that they need to finally make a real splash on signings to get to that next level and threaten to head to the Premier League for the first time in the club's long history.

When you look at how Portsmouth owner Michael Eisner has made his billions, it's no great shock that few second-tier sides can boast a wealthier chief than the New York native - even if, once again, that isn't always reflected in the club's transfer activity.

As per the Los Angeles Business Journal in 2024, Eisner has accumulated a net worth of $3.8 billion (£2.83 billion), having formerly held the role of Disney's CEO for more than 20 years before entering the world of football ownership by taking over Pompey nine years ago.

FLW takes a look at which Championship clubs have the highest wage bill heading into the new season

John Mousinho hasn't been totally without backing in recent years, and Pompey's exile from the Championship has ended under Eisner's ownership, but his investment continues to be patient and methodical without throwing everything towards bringing Premier League football back to Fratton Park - although the summer of 2026 has definitely seen a more 'shackles off' approach at Fratton Park.

We know far less about Charlton Athletic owner Joshua Friedman, who is the majority shareholder of a consortium - Global Football Partners - that completed a takeover to purchase the South London outfit from Thomas Sandgaard in the summer of 2023.

Indeed, official net worth estimates of Friedman are sparse. However, if claims of $5 billion (£3.72 billion) are to be believed, then Charlton very much have a wealthy board, and that has shone through in recent times.

The Addicks' investment has amplified since returning to the Championship through the League One play-offs in May of last year, which preceded - as per Transfermarkt - a summer spending spree under Nathan Jones worth €11.62 million (£10.07 million) as the likes of Rob Apter, Thomas Kaminski, Charlie Kelman and Harvey Knibbs all made their way to the Valley and ultimately helped to keep the side afloat.

There are a number of shareholders on the board at West Ham, and until June, the two largest stakes belonged to controversial chairman David Sullivan and his family, and Daniel Kretinsky, at 38.8% and 27% respectively.

That changed though recently, with Czech businessman Kretinsky and his consortium's stake rising to 43 per cent after a deal was struck with Vanessa Gold - and that could lead to a more ambitious Hammers going into 2026-27.

As per the Sunday Times Rich List of 2025 (via the BBC), Kretinsky's wealth comes in at $10 billion (£8.68 billion), which is a clear second in the Championship when it comes to riches.

Sullivan has ploughed heavy investment into West Ham over the years, much of which was done alongside the late David Gold, although he's hardly a popular figure at the London Stadium owing to the decision to move out of Upton Park and, more recently, a seemingly-endless series of big-money signings who have failed to deliver - and that's ultimately why the East Londoners will be playing Championship football next season for the first time since 2012.

Under Kretinsky's largest stakeholding though, things may be different, and fans will hope that the owner of Czech energy company EPH and also the owner of Royal Mail will actually be a majority owner when Sullivan decides he wants to sell up his share entirely.

Wolves have the richest owners in the Championship overall, with the Old Gold enduring something of a rollercoaster journey throughout the Fosun Group's 10-year reign in charge at Molineux.

Made up of majority stakeholder Guo Guanchang, Fosun Group CEO Wang Qunbin and interim executive chairman Nathan Shi, Fosun's net worth is not publicly known. The Chinese conglomerate is seriously wealthy, though, and according to Companies Market Cap in June 2025, the total net worth sits at a stunning £20.53 billion.

Who is the best Championship owner? Let us know in the comments!

Following a tumultous couple of years in the Premier League, which saw Wolves relegated in dead-last in 25/26, the Molineux faithful will now be hoping that Fosun can show the same level of investment and ambition back in the Championship just as they did when the side last graced the division, going up as champions after signing the likes of Ruben Neves and the late Diogo Jota.

#2101. Fabrizio Romano shares latest on Martinez contract after explosive rant

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

The Argentinian defender has also apologized to the United higher ups as well over his comments, as shared by Fabrizio Romano.

Lisandro Martinez has held discussions with Jason Wilcox and Michael Carrick after speaking out following United’s 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid.

Martinez had questioned whether Carrick was backed enough in the summer and suggested the club needed changes.

Fabrizio Romano has now confirmed that United consider the matter resolved for now and expect Martinez to remain available for selection.

Speaking about the situation on his YouTube channel, as quoted by Football 365, Romano explained why Martinez’s comments caused concern inside the club.

“He spoke very strongly after the game against Atletico Madrid, which Man Utd lost. It was a very negative moment for the Red Devils. We know that Licha was very strong in his comments. He said that Michael Carrick was not backed enough during the summer transfer window.”

Romano added that Martinez had spoken directly to those at the club after the incident.

“Licha apologised to Man Utd as a club. He spoke to the directors, he spoke to Jason Wilcox, and he spoke to Michael Carrick, who was also involved in this conversation.”

“So, the underlying message remains the same. Lisandro is apologising for the way he expressed himself after a game during a difficult moment for Man Utd, but there was a discussion about the substance of what he said.”

Romano also revealed that United had imposed a financial penalty on the centre-back. However, the punishment does not appear to involve removing him from the squad.

“According to the information available tonight, Lisandro Martinez has been fined.”

He added that Martinez is expected to return to the squad as normal, with the fine considered sufficient punishment for the incident.

“The internal discussion also helped to resolve all the issues. For Man Utd, the case is closed.”

That should bring some immediate clarity to the situation, although questions remain about how the episode could affect Martinez’s longer-term position at Old Trafford.

Romano also pointed towards Martinez’s contract, which expires next summer, with United holding an option to extend it.

“So, let’s see what is going to happen there. For sure, this is the kind of situation that will have an impact on the situation surrounding Lisandro, but we have to see what happens next in terms of future transfers and everything else.”

#2100. Arsenal star Max Dowman smashes Jude Bellingham's record - but a less-familiar name should catch Thomas Tuchel's eye ahead of Euro 2028: THINGS WE LEARNED from England U21's defeat to Portugal

Published: 16:46 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 18:41 EST, 13 November 2026

Max Dowman smashed Jude Bellingham's record on an icy cold night in Bristol to become the youngest player to ever play for England's Under-21s.

The 16-year-old was sent on with 30 minutes to go by Lee Carsley in a move that energised an Ashton Gate crowd that went home frustrated after a 1-0 defeat inflicted by Afonso Moreira's first half goal.

But this was to be Dowman's night, smashing the previous record set by Bellingham when he made his England Under-21 debut against Kosovo in 2020 aged 17 years, two months and six days old. Dowman does not turn 17 until December 31.

Under-21s boss Lee Carsley has been keen long before this international break to try to shield Dowman from the weight of expectation.

But on he came, replacing the lively Amario Cozier-Duberry with a smile on his face and a quiet confidence that he didn't take long to show off, bursting past two Portuguese markers before four huddled together to gang up on him.

Breaking records is nothing new to a player that already holds one for being the Premier League's youngest-ever goalscorer, thanks to his goal against Everton last season.

Max Dowman wrote his name into the record books once more, playing for England Under-21s

Dowman came on to rich applause on a cold night in Bristol to shatter Jude Bellingham's record

The Arsenal teenager was lively playing off the right as he now targets the 2027 U21 Euros

Dowman is both the youngest player to ever win the Premier League and his outing in the Champions League against Slavia Prague last season saw the then-15-year-old become the youngest-ever player to appear in that competition.

By the time next summer's European Championships, which England will attempt to win for a third successive time, rolls around, rising star Dowman could well have earned the right to be this team's main man.

'We've only got three games left before the Euros [next summer],' Carsley explained.

'So it's important that he puts himself in the shop window to be on the plane.

'It's important that he keeps playing well, getting minutes, showing a really good attitude, like he has done.

'I thought he was outstanding when he came on tonight. I thought all of the subs made a real impact.

'I thought Max was unlucky not to get an assist... he made a great pass to Mikey Moore.

'He took up some really good positions, both in the 10 and out wide, he's got a big future ahead.'

His immense talent was one reason why Arsenal sent Ethan Nwaneri, who Dowman played alongside for part of his cameo, to Marseille on loan, and then similarly to Borussia Dortmund, eager not to block the 16-year-old's pathway.

Carsley knows the diamond he has on his hands and will want to take great care in helping polish a player that this crowd, this England team and this management group know has genuine world class potential.

Speaking of Nwaneri, this felt like a big camp for him. A big camp in the sense that he's falling down the pecking order at Dortmund and is back with a manager that has been so vital in his development.

Nwaneri was part of that 2025 group that won the Euros in front of Thomas Tuchel and he'll have seen the likes of Elliot Anderson and Alex Scott kick on to get to the seniors.

As previously mentioned, Nwaneri was moved out of the way by Arsenal to aid Dowman's development, not an easy pill for a player as talented as he is to stomach when his own development journey is at such a critical juncture given he is, to the surprise of many, still only 19.

'I think we have to remember his age as well,' Carsley added when asked about Nwaneri by Daily Mail Sport.

'He's very young is Ethan and he's another one that we've got a lot of hope for. He's got a lot of potential.'

Ethan Nwaneri was pushed to the side at Arsenal to benefit Dowman but England is different

Lee Carsley has been a crucial figure in the development of Nwaneri and this camp was timely

It was telling that even when Dowman came on, even with the groundswell of excitement at his introduction, it was Carsley's call to keep Nwaneri in his preferred No 10 position with Dowman slotting in on the right.

Nwaneri has only started four games on loan at Dortmund this season and has not managed a single start in the Champions League.

His close control, his quick burst over five yards and the fluidity of his movement was a timely reminder that yes, Dowman is the rising star everyone came out to see, but Nwaneri won't get pushed to the side again without a fight.

Amario Cozier-Duberry is a name not all will be familiar with but come next summer, with the Euros in his sights and promotion to the Premier League on the agenda with Middlesbrough, that could all be about to change.

The 21-year-old has had to be very patient, waiting until last month to make his debut at this level after years of finding himself overlooked.

Here, in what was just his third Under-21 appearance, he showed over the course of 61 minutes why the days of being looked past should be over.

One of the big frustrations in the FA right now at Under-21 level is the lack of touchline wingers. Rio Ngumoha, still only 18, has never been capped at the level and has instead been catapulted into the first team, while many, like Ethan Nwaneri, prefer playing inside.

'The more we can get our wide players one v one the better,' Carsley said. 'I think sometimes we leave them isolated and the opposition are able to double up on them.

Amario Cozier-Duberry is not a household name at international level but his talent is immense

'It's important that our game plan can't just be to get the ball wide and hope for the best.'

Dowman, on in place of Cozier-Duberry is a 10, rather than a right winger which is where he came on, and so a player like Cozier-Duberry, who is on loan at Middlesbrough from Brighton & Hove Albion, is worth his weight in gold.

Here in Bristol he was routinely drawing two defenders and at times three; Portugal knew full well how a quick flip-flap of the ball, or one clipped pass over the top, was enough for the Englishman to take the top off the back-line.

His loan at Bolton Wanderers last season complicated an international journey that has seen him play at Under-16, Under-17, Under-18, Under-19 and Under-20 level, but that's all in the past.

England need a genuine, pacy threat out wide if they are to win a third straight Euros. Cozier-Duberry showed here exactly why he should be it.

The favourites are clear, though: Endrick and Nicolo Tresoldi.

Speaking on Fabrizio Romano’s YouTube channel, Matteo Moretto provided an update on the Rossoneri’s pursuit for both forwards and whether either was progressing, as MilanNews relayed.

“Although Mourinho continues to say that Endrick will stay at Real Madrid, the truth is that the player has the ball right now. If the player decides to tell Real Madrid that he wants to try a new experience to grow and play, Real Madrid will not object. And I can tell you that these are precisely the indications.

TEAMtalk transfer insider Graeme Bailey has suggested Michael Carrick could bring the Argentine straight back into the team for the trip to Elland Road. The fixture is expected to be a hostile occasion, making Martinez’s potential involvement an interesting one.

Bailey also dismissed suggestions that Martinez’s comments were an attack on Michael Carrick, insisting the defender and his teammates continue to support the head coach.

#2096. Charlton Athletic boss Nathan Jones left unhappy at FA rule change

Charlton Athletic boss Nathan Jones is one of "a number" of head coaches in the top four leagues in England to have objected to the yellow card rules bestowed upon managers.

It has been the case since the 2018/19 campaign that cautions could be shown to the dugouts in the EFL, with the Premier League following suit the following year. Traditionally, a manager would have to receive four yellow cards before they would receive a touchline ban.

However, in an update to the rules ahead of the 2023/24 term, the FA introduced a 'Participant Behaviour Charter' to maintain a positive environment across the top-flight, the EFL, the Women's Super League and the National League System (Steps 1-4).

The new charter brought in the current rule that a manager only has to be shown three yellow cards to receive a touchline ban, with the cut-off point being the 37th game of the season. Unsurprisingly, Jones, one of the more animated coaches in the game, is against that.

According to Standard Sport, Charlton boss Nathan Jones is among several head coaches who don't like the reduction to how many yellow cards lead to a touchline for a manager.

Managers across the 92 had a meeting recently to discuss the effectiveness of these rules, and Jones, among others, believes that the threshold is incredibly short, especially with managers under much more pressure and scrutiny than ever before, it seems.

Additionally, in comparison to players, who pick up a one-match suspension for five yellow cards by the 19th game of the season, and a two-match ban if they collect 10 by the 37th, a touchline ban for just three cautions by the 37th for a manager seems incredibly harsh.

Head coaches find themselves booked if they are caught out of their technical areas, and they also receive yellow cards if there are any infringements in the dugout that a referee cannot attribute to one person. As the 'most senior' member of staff, they are the ones responsible for controlling things.

Nathan Jones will be one of the few managers who fall victim to these cards, and he is understandably looking for the rules to be relaxed.

Ultimately, certain head coaches will feel that these rules almost limit how well they can do their jobs, especially someone like Jones, who isn't afraid to let his emotions show.

The Welshman was seen almost joining a late attack against Hull City last season, and hung off the dugout after his side scored a late equaliser against Burnley this term, among other crazy things that only someone like Jones is associated with.

Having his actions limited on the sidelines may be detrimental to how much he can motivate his side, especially given how infrequent these sanctions can be.

FLW has debated which 15 fanbases generate the best atmospheres and more inside their home stadiums

Not every departure from a technical area is a yellow card, as Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta, another very animated manager, rightly pointed out in late October after he admitted he was clipping up infringements from his fellow coaches after he was accused of spending more time out of his little box than others were.

So, managers already feel as if they are walking on eggshells; such is the nature of the job, but sanctions like these can often make it even more of a nervous place.

However, despite Jones and other managers' grumbles, the FA can point to a 17% decrease in technical area cautions since the start of the 2023/24 campaign when the three-yellow-card rule was implemented.

What do you think about the manager yellow card rules? Let us know in the comments.

The numbers indicate that things are working, but again, managers may point to the infrequency of the rules as the reason for that. Not every infringement should be a yellow card, but the reasons why they are being handed out aren't something that coaches agree on.

Time will tell whether the Charlton boss, and others who oppose the rule change, will have their way and see the yellow card threshold increase once more, but with the success of the charter so far, it may be difficult for them to persuade the FA.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#2095. Leeds vs Man Utd preview: Team news, form, injuries and where to watch

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Leeds United welcome Manchester United to Elland Road on Sunday, with both sides looking to put a difficult run of results behind them and get their Premier League season on track.

Leeds United suffered a 2-1 defeat away to Arsenal last weekend despite James Justin scoring to put them in front in the 55th minute.

Manchester United also dropped points in the Premier League, drawing 1-1 with Tottenham, before losing 2-0 to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League away from home.

Michael Carrick’s side have struggled to find consistency in recent weeks and have come under immense pressure to get in results. The Whites meanwhile will hope that home advantage can make the difference when United face their bitter rivals on Elland Road.

Leeds have recorded one win, two draws and two defeats in their last five matches in all competitions. Their best result came against Newcastle, where they won, but a 6-3 defeat to Chelsea in the Carabao Cup and the loss to Arsenal have left them searching for a response.

Manchester United have also won just once in their last five matches. Their 4-0 Champions League victory over Sabah FK was the only comfortable win, but defeats to Manchester City and Atletico Madrid, alongside draws against Fulham and Tottenham, have raised questions about their form and Michael Carrick.

Leeds are waiting on Dan James, who returned from international duty with a back problem and missed the Arsenal game. Joe Rodon remains sidelined with a hamstring injury and is not expected back in full training until next month. Harry Wilson could return after being an unused substitute last weekend. Mateo Joseph is also among Leeds’ absentees.

Manchester United have their own concerns. Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo are doubts after picking up issues against Tottenham and missing Tuesday’s trip to Madrid. Benjamin Sesko remains unavailable with a recurring shin problem, while Patrick Dorgu is expected to be out until late November. Manuel Ugarte is recovering from knee surgery, and Noussair Mazraoui is a doubt with a back problem.

There is better news regarding Matthijs de Ligt, who could return to contention. Leny Yoro is also available for selection despite his Champions League suspension.

The match takes place at Elland Road on Sunday, October 18. Kick-off is scheduled for 2 pm BST (1pm GMT).

UK viewers can watch the game live on Sky Sports Main Event, with coverage beginning at 1 pm BST.

#2092. Chelsea World Cup Knockout Load Gives Xabi Alonso Pre-Season Problem

Chelsea’s World Cup contingent has moved from a group-stage watchlist into a genuine Xabi Alonso planning problem.

Chelsea’s own tournament update confirms that Enzo Fernandez, Mike Penders, Moises Caicedo, Kendry Paez, Malo Gusto and Jorrel Hato have reached the Round of 32.

England have also progressed after their final Group L win over Panama, which keeps Reece James and Trevoh Chalobah inside the wider knockout picture.

For supporters, that is a status marker. For Alonso, it is where summer pride starts to become pre-season compression.

The concern is not simply volume. It is where the minutes are landing.

Enzo has not missed a minute for Argentina, while Caicedo has remained central for Ecuador and captained them in the 2-1 win over Germany.

Those are not fringe workloads. They are the two midfield profiles Chelsea have built large parts of their control game around.

Alonso’s first Chelsea pre-season was always going to demand clarity through the middle of the pitch.

Instead, the players most central to that reset are still operating in knockout football.

Caicedo’s Ecuador role is the cleanest example. Read Chelsea has already assessed how his captaincy display against Germany strengthened his leadership case, but the next layer is more complicated.

Every additional knockout tie gives him more tournament rhythm, more authority and more fatigue.

Argentina’s route against Cape Verde keeps him on a glamorous stage at exactly the moment Chelsea need to settle his role, mood and tactical responsibilities under Alonso.

If Madrid-related noise continues around him, the club cannot afford a sluggish July handover.

Reece James started England’s first two matches before a hamstring issue ruled him out of the Panama game, according to the Guardian.

England still topped the group and moved into a last-32 tie with DR Congo, but James’ situation is exactly the kind of detail Chelsea’s medical team will monitor closely.

Chelsea have already had to plan around a large World Cup group.

The broader issue was clear in Read Chelsea’s earlier pre-season workload piece, but the knockout stage sharpens it because the returns will now be staggered.

Enzo brings a maximum group-stage load. Caicedo brings captaincy responsibility and heavy Ecuador minutes.

James brings knockout qualification mixed with another hamstring-management question.

Gusto and Hato remain tied to France and the Netherlands, while Penders and Paez are still absorbing tournament environments before club reintegration.

That is a spine issue, not a fringe issue.

Alonso needs automatisms in possession, spacing around the double pivot, clearer full-back behaviour and pressing triggers from midfield.

Those details do not bed in properly when key players arrive in drips after a major summer tournament.

Players returning from knockout football can bring competitive sharpness that closed-door friendlies cannot replicate.

Caicedo captaining Ecuador through pressure games matters. Enzo playing high-leverage minutes for Argentina matters.

Gusto and Hato absorbing tournament detail also helps Chelsea’s defensive reset.

But Chelsea cannot treat every tournament minute as clean preparation.

Alonso must decide who returns straight into tactical work, who needs a genuine pause and who can handle August without creating an avoidable injury bill by September.

That is where the James situation feels central.

If Chelsea’s captain carries a World Cup hamstring warning, the club’s right-sided structure becomes more than a selection debate.

It becomes an availability question that touches Gusto, the wider defensive rebuild and the need for control from midfield.

Read Chelsea has already looked at James’ captaincy test under Alonso, and the injury layer now makes that test sharper.

This is the hidden cost of a strong international footprint.

Chelsea want players good enough to survive deep into tournaments.

Alonso now has to make sure that status does not leave his first league weeks short of the very control those players are meant to provide.

#2091. Tare discusses new Milan direction, limitations in his role and ‘jealousy’: “Better late than never”

Igli Tare has spoken without holding anything back about his time at AC Milan, explaining his frustration with several things.

When Tare arrived, many Milan fans were happy to see someone with Serie A experience oversee the project and whilst his first season didn’t end how anyone had hoped, he wasn’t seen as a major issue.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

So, when it was announced that he was part of a complete overturning of the management, there was a bit of a surprise, even if it did feel inevitable at one point.

With the overhaul of changes in the summer, one does wonder what Tare would have done differently, especially with suggestions that his hands were tied in the mercato last season. Nevertheless,

Speaking on Sky Sport’s ‘Calcio Unplugged’, Igli Tare revealed all to Gianluca Di Marzio and Stefano Borghi in an in-depth interview about his time with the Diavolo, as Radio Rossonera has relayed.

“Today is the first time I’ve spoken out after all these months. The wound of not having reached the Champions League is still enormous, and since I arrived at Milan – also questioning myself with the type of contract I signed – the objective couldn’t be only the Champions League; otherwise I wouldn’t have understood where I was.”

“It was great because he was the one who convinced me. He had such a huge desire to join Milan. I wanted to video chat before going to see him because I couldn’t believe it. But after five minutes, I knew in my head that he was the player Milan really lacked.

“Not just because of his qualities, but as a man and as a figure that that team didn’t have. He never said no. A photo with a child, an autograph, a meeting, talking to someone… He never said no. These are the things that humility is key to in life.

“I’m proud to have brought a great champion to Milan. In my opinion, if he wants, he can play another two seasons without any problem. He never missed a training session. Sometimes we were the ones to stop him because he was always there, ready. Loving football at that age is truly an honour.”

Is it a characteristic of the champion or is it a generational issue? Today’s champions seem to have a different mentality:

“Today we live in the age of social media. At 16, you’re already a footballer who can earn millions of euros. Living this way, you have the problem of not only managing a player, who is still a child, but you have to manage the business they bring with them: family, agents, girlfriends…

“These are obstacles that didn’t exist back then. We were a generation that played in the streets. Back then, our parents beat us to get us to come home. Today, however, it’s to get them out of the house because they spend all day in front of computers.

“This aspect has been lost a bit, but it’s our fault. Education and discipline are the key to success.”

Fullkrug. He performed poorly in Milan, but in the Bundesliga he’s scoring a lot and is the top scorer. How do you explain that?

“It’s simple. He came to us after a tough time in England, with a lot of scepticism. And then, right away, he broke his toe. No one ever said he’d been having injections on the bone for two months just to train, let alone to play.

“I knew he was a centre forward that the team was missing; given his characteristics and his interpretation of the game, his qualities were unquestionable. Just two years before coming to Milan, he’d played in the Champions League final, playing a key role in a competition with Borussia Dortmund.

“There are situations where, for a player, even a very important one, it matters how you feel. If you feel appreciated, valued, taken into consideration… When you play for a club like Milan, the weight of the shirt is completely different than when you play for other clubs.

“You feel it from the first day you join. I had no doubt that he could be what he’s demonstrating now.”

“We tried to sign him back in June. We made a first attempt. In the final days of the transfer window, another important name we tried to sign was Akanji. The Champions League was crucial for both of them. They turned him down, not because of the club’s importance, but because he wasn’t playing in the Champions League.

“Then the opportunity arose again at the end of August for Rabiot. Defeat against Cremonese? No, we had already decided to bring him. It was just a matter of contract details.”

“It was difficult for us because we decided to change the formation five days before the transfer window closed. Switching from a 4-3-3 to a three-man defense meant we were having a really hard time finding a quality player in the last five days.

“We were a bit unlucky, first with the Akanji story and then with Liverpool’s Joe Gomez… Guehi’s move from Crystal Palace to Liverpool fell through, and at the last minute they—we already had the deal ready, we were just waiting for this to happen—made a step back. And to avoid being left without a central defender at the last minute, we signed Odogu as a promising player.”

On not being able to reach the Champions League and not being able to continue his work at Milan…

“This is the first time today, after all these months, that I’ve spoken about this… The wound of not reaching the Champions League is still enormous. I think that from the first day I arrived at Milan, even in the way I signed—I questioned myself with the type of contract.

“I said, ‘If I have to come only for the Champions League objective, then I don’t understand where I’ve come from.’ Milan has a different story. I had to go through a trial. The disappointment is that those who run the club didn’t understand how much time people needed, which is now being done, rightly so.

“That is to say, it takes several transfer sessions to get a competitive team ready to win. At the beginning, I felt the responsibility to put the pieces together immediately, because after the defeat in the Coppa Italia final the year before, there were some important signs.

“I didn’t know where to start. But I think we did an important job last summer, we sold for a lot and also signed 10 new players. Then you need time to integrate, learn new philosophies and create a cohesive group, hungry to win.

“Until March-April, we were a group with difficulties, but we were at the top of the table. Then in the last 10 matchdays, we had a mental breakdown, also due to other external dynamics, which I don’t want to discuss here, which had a significant impact.

“Internal or external dynamics? External to the team. But we also have some blame: myself first and foremost, along with Max [Allegri].

“We had to be a little more attentive to certain dynamics. We needed to be more present with the team to ultimately lead them to the final result. Isolation is the wrong word; I don’t believe in these things. I believe in teamwork; I believe in cohesion: from the club to the team.

“When this happens, you transmit it to the team. When these situations become possible, you could also see it in the team’s results, because the players are very attentive. Sometimes we think they have other interests, but they pay attention to everything that comes out. They follow everything very carefully and transmit it.

“Instilling serenity… How can you convey serenity? When, in difficult moments, you show that you believe in the project more than before. Sometimes I missed this feeling, a lack of something that could give us the final push.”

But despite this, did you think you could continue? Does this farewell after only a year feel like a stab in the back?

“Look, I would have asked for a round table where we could all sit down together and analyze everything. Then they could have just said ‘no, thanks’… But I respect the decision they made. I accept it with great regret, but I’ve never questioned it because there’s someone above me who has to decide, including for the fate of the club.

“And when they decide to take a different path, you have to accept it. I know things could have gone differently, even much better. I’ll always be a Milan fan, even after an experience like that.”

Was AC Milan a team that needed the constant presence of a manager or coach to avoid letting itself go as it later did?

“The feeling I had at the beginning was that this leadership was a bit lacking. The arrival of Modric—and another of our goals was also Granit Xhaka, Leverkusen’s captain—was precisely to bring real players into the group, with important characteristics and capable of leading others.

“Granit didn’t arrive; Luka arrived, who has a different way of being a leader: he does it in silence and with his attitude on the pitch. I had the opportunity to meet Mike Maignan: an extraordinary guy, a soul who cares deeply about the AC Milan shirt.

“Gabbia is another extraordinary guy; he lives for this club. Rabiot too… His experience spoke for itself. The great disappointment is that I expected something more in terms of responsibility and leadership from Pulisic: he’s a top-class player with unquestionable qualities. But in terms of performance, things happened that I had never experienced in my career…

“Like Gimenez: an extraordinary guy with numbers that spoke for themselves; for a year he failed to score a goal. Then it happened that Pulisic didn’t score for six months. He scored a goal. Then Leao didn’t score for four months.

“Situations that are hard to come by in football have happened… It can happen that you don’t score for a month, two months, but that long a period of time also affected the team’s final performance.

“Losing a match against Cagliari the way we did, 2-1, I think was the worst match of my life. The feeling and the disappointment I felt towards the fans in the stadium that night is something I will never forget for the rest of my life.”

If Cardinale had been the Cardinale he is today, the one who is also physically present, would you still be AC ​​Milan’s DS?

“I can’t answer that question; he has to answer it. I can say that I remember when the Jashari negotiations were going on… I had just landed in Rome and I was very pleased when he called me because he wanted to understand what was happening in that negotiation.

“I explained all the dynamics to him and I really liked that he said, ‘Anything you need, if you have to spend a little more, let me know because I’m here.’ Then during that process I never had the chance to talk to him, even intentionally.

“There were other people above me who I never wanted to bypass. I never had a direct relationship with him, and the possibility of a discussion would have helped everyone. Not me, but everyone. By putting all the problems and dynamics on the table, we could have resolved things much sooner. But I think it’s a new experience for Cardinale.

“He’s had experience in other sports in America. Now he’s done something important, taking responsibility and putting his face on the line. I would have preferred to have had that presence even when I was there because it would have been very useful. But for the Milan, better late than never.

“Now, for better or worse, he will make his own decisions and responsibilities. I think that for him, too, the best interests of Milan come first.”

Was Leao a problem or a resource in your mind?

“I knew him from the outside. When I had the chance to meet him in person, I thought he was an extraordinary guy. I truly loved him as a person, like everyone else. But he was the player from whom we all expected something more. I think football was no longer a priority for him. That’s the key to understanding him.”

“I think a bit about his life outside of football. Music, fashion, things… But I never doubted the sense of belonging he had towards Milan. You could sense that he loved playing for Milan and was suffering from not performing.

“He had many physical problems… First a calf, then a bit of pubalgia… He always played with his hands under control. I always tried to have individual conversations with him more than with any other Milan player.

“Every time I spoke to him, I left with a positive feeling. I sensed that he wanted to. But sometimes wanting isn’t enough.”

Was there a chance that Leao would leave during your summer too?

“A concrete offer never came for him. Regarding the other transfers, it’s not just Tare’s job. When I arrived – even at Lazio – I was a bit alone, but I tried to involve all the members of the club to give him the importance he needed to build a sense of belonging and responsibility. I think I did a very good job, together with Furlani, Ibra, and Moncada.

“We achieved significant sales figures, in a year when we weren’t even in the Champions League. Thanks to the work we did last summer, investments were made this year, with the money we had at the time. I really believe in teamwork.

“I said it even before the Coppa Italia match against Bari; I asked to speak to convey the importance of the work of the people within the club because it was right that way. Then afterwards, it’s human…

“They were coming off a bad year, when two cumbersome figures like Tare and Allegri arrive, and everyone was talking about Tare and Allegri, some disappointment was understandable. I understood the feeling they had, but I could… There was little to do about it.

“For me, it was a new path, a new opportunity. It was essential to work as a team and present ourselves as a real company.”

#2090. Jamie Carragher names Man Utd Star who impressed him against Leeds

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United had a difficult evening once again as they were held to a 1-1 draw at Leeds United. Pressure mounts on Michael Carrick as United have just 7 points from 7 games.

Manchester United took the lead through Bryan Mbeumo in the first half, with the forward finishing Youri Tielemans’ excellent cross from the right. However, the visitors couldn’t hold on to their advantage as Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised for Leeds United from a corner.

The draw extended United’s frustrating run of results, leaving Michael Carrick still searching for the consistency his side need.

Carragher, though, believes there were positives to take from the trip, particularly one performance at the back.

Jamie Carragher has singled out Harry Maguire for praise after Manchester United drew 1-1 with Leeds United at Elland Road on Sunday.

Speaking on Sky Sports, the former Liverpool defender admitted that picking up a point at Elland Road was not necessarily a bad result in isolation, even if United’s recent form made it feel like a missed opportunity.

“Going away to Leeds is going to be tricky for any team except for Manchester City and Arsenal at the moment,” Carragher said.

“A lot of teams will take a point at Leeds this season but the problem for Manchester United is the results have been so poor that they need to start winning games so it almost feels like two points dropped.”

Carragher then turned his attention to Maguire, who he felt played a major role in keeping United in the game when Leeds began to push for a winner.

“But in isolation, getting a point at Leeds is a decent result. I thought Harry Maguire was fantastic, especially in the second half.”

Leeds United grew into the contest after Calvert-Lewin brought them level, putting United under pressure during the closing stages. Carragher felt Maguire’s efforts in defence helped prevent the visitors from falling apart.

“After Leeds got that goal back there was a stage of the game where it felt like Man United could go under, but Maguire at the back held it together for them. He was fantastic.”

The result may feel like another opportunity missed for Carrick, but Maguire’s performance gave United something positive to take away from Elland Road.

#2089. Malo Gusto’s Kante Lesson Gives Chelsea A £75m Xabi Alonso Decision

Malo Gusto’s World Cup has suddenly become more than a France subplot for Chelsea. It is now a live assessment of whether Xabi Alonso inherits a right-back worth protecting, reshaping or trading at the peak of his market.

Chelsea’s own interview with Gusto this week underlined the human part of that equation. The 23-year-old spoke about learning from N’Golo Kante, calling the former Blue one of the best midfielders France have produced and stressing the value of his example on and off the pitch.

That matters because Kante is not just a nostalgic reference point. He remains the standard Chelsea supporters still use when judging humility, intensity and reliability in a high-pressure dressing room.

For Gusto, those qualities arrive at a decisive moment. Reports around the player’s future claim Chelsea value him at around £75million, with the imminent Marco Palestra deal creating a more crowded full-back picture.

That number looks aggressive, but the logic is clear. Gusto is young, capped by France, under contract, Premier League-tested and capable of playing in several defensive structures.

🚨🚨| NEW: Chelsea are open to selling Malo Gusto this summer, with his agent already in 𝐓𝐀𝐋𝐊𝐒 with Manchester City and Inter. Chelsea will only sell if their valuation is met.{@siphillipssport} pic.twitter.com/vNR2bWud9F

The easiest reading of Gusto’s Kante comments is sentimental. It should not be.

For Alonso, who officially begins work on July 1, the important detail is what those comments say about the player Chelsea have been developing.

Gusto has not always looked completely settled at Stamford Bridge. His best games have carried thrust, speed and recovery power, while his less convincing spells have raised questions about final-ball quality and defensive concentration.

That uncertainty is exactly why the next coach matters.

Alonso’s previous teams have leaned heavily on wide players who can receive under pressure, attack space early and still protect the back line when possession breaks down. Gusto has the athletic base for that job.

The test is whether his decision-making can be refined enough to make him a structural piece rather than a rotation asset.

That is where the Kante reference lands with force. Chelsea do not need Gusto to imitate Kante’s position. They need him to absorb the same professional standard: repeat actions, clean defensive choices, no wasted emotion and total commitment to the collective rhythm.

The Marco Palestra deal changes the right side of Chelsea’s squad immediately. Read Chelsea has already examined how Palestra’s arrival offers a tactical clue over Alonso’s defensive plans, and that pressure is now sharpened by market noise around Gusto.

Chelsea can frame the situation in two ways.

One is profit-led. If a club comes close to the reported £75million level, selling a player signed from Lyon for a much lower fee becomes a powerful PSR lever.

The other is football-led. If Alonso sees Gusto as a high-upside wing-back who fits his model, selling him just as the coaching environment becomes more suitable would carry long-term risk.

The complication is Reece James. The captain’s fitness issues, including his current England hamstring concern, mean Chelsea still need genuine right-sided depth.

Palestra may be part of the future, but Gusto is already part of the present. Chelsea have too often needed emergency solutions in that area to treat proven depth lightly.

That is why Read Chelsea’s recent look at James awaiting hamstring scan results matters in this debate. Right-back remains one of the most talented areas of the squad, but also one of the least straightforward.

This is why Gusto’s France rhythm is more valuable than a simple tournament diary entry. Chelsea are watching a player operate inside an elite international camp, learn from a club legend and handle a public transfer valuation that can change his status overnight.

Alonso’s first decision does not have to be final, but it does have to be clear.

If Gusto stays, he needs a defined role early in pre-season and a pathway that makes sense alongside Palestra and James. If Chelsea sell, they need to do it at a number that justifies weakening one of the few squad areas where youth, speed and top-level experience already overlap.

Gusto’s Kante lesson, then, is not just a feel-good Chelsea connection. It is a reminder of the standard Alonso must demand before deciding whether £75million is a price to accept or a warning sign that Chelsea should hold firm.

#2088. Lots to work on but Pocognoli firmly believes Scotland ARE on the right track under his stewardship

Published: 18:44 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 19:02 EST, 13 November 2026

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli admitted his side were far from perfect in their Nations League win over North Macedonia – but he believes they ARE moving in the right direction under his stewardship.

The victory puts the Scots one point behind second-placed Slovenia in Group B1, ahead of Monday’s trip to runaway leaders Switzerland.

John McGinn notched a second-half double to secure a hard-earned second win of this campaign and Pocognoli’s first in front of the Hampden crowd.

‘We knew before the game that it [a win] will help to build a winning culture,’ he said. ‘And would make the work through the week end with a good feeling.

‘In terms of what we produced on the pitch, I know exactly what we worked on this week. I’m quite satisfied about what I see in some moments of the game, about the work on the ball and off the ball.

‘It was not always perfect but we created a lot of chances that we should score and maybe have a better feeling of the game.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his Hampden win as Scots boss after a 2-1 win over North Macedonia

Stalwarts John McGinn (left) and Andy Robertson applaud the Hampden crowd at full-time

‘Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive. We recover a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition.

‘We created a big chance for Billy [Gilmour] from this also. So that’s a new approach of the game.

‘We created chances and we had a lot of pressure in the side of Macedonia. After the first goal I think we need to learn not to drop the intensity. Because after the first goal for five minutes I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus. So, it’s something that we need to fix.’

Asked whether his side need to be more clinical, Pocognoli added: ‘Yes, probably. But I prefer to talk about this with creating a lot of chances. We should score two or three. And probably we should have kept a clean sheet. So that’s really the critical aspect and the demanding aspect.

‘But it’s part of the challenge and we are early in the challenge to try to fix this for the future.’

Talisman McGinn put the Scots ahead on 54 minutes before Elmin Rastoder headed the visitors level against the run of play shortly after, with McGinn then stepping up to convert what turned out to be the winning penalty after a foul on Ben Gannon-Doak with 16 to play.

The Aston Villa midfielder has now taken his tally to 24 for the international team – just six behind legends Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law.

His manager is confident that it is only a matter of time before the 32-year-old is standing alone as his nation’s top scorer, and believes McGinn will have plenty of opportunities to smash the record playing in his team.

John McGinn scored from the penalty spot to clinch an unconvincing victory

He said: ‘I’m more focused on the collective challenge and goals. And I believe if we can build something nice around the collective, then John will one day break the record.

‘We created a lot of chances through these five [Nations League] games together. The individual record is important, but I always focus on the collective package.’

McGinn admitted that chasing the record is in the back of his mind and stressed his relief that he’s back among the goals after a lean spell at international level.

‘It’s been something that’s been in the back of my head, but obviously the results haven’t been the way we’ve wanted,’ said McGinn.

‘The team come first, but whether it’s myself, Scottie (McTominay), Che (Adams), anyone that’s going on the scoresheet at the minute, we’ll take it.

‘It’s been a bit of a dry patch for me over the past year or two on the goal front, so I’m delighted to get back on that trail and hopefully the same again Monday.

‘I feel good. I’ve still got many years to go, but the first priority is getting Scotland back to another major tournament and we’ll take it from there.’

#2086. Senegal Knockout Tie Gives Chelsea A Double Xabi Alonso Audit

Chelsea’s World Cup watch has moved beyond simple minutes management.

Senegal’s Round-of-32 meeting with Belgium now gives Xabi Alonso a live read on two very different development tracks.

Nicolas Jackson’s attacking authority is the immediate question. Mamadou Sarr’s defensive readiness is the longer-term one.

Chelsea confirmed that Senegal kept their knockout hopes alive with a 5-0 win over Iraq, with Jackson featuring from the bench.

Senegal have since moved into the knockouts, where they face Belgium in Seattle on Wednesday 1 July.

Jackson and Sarr travel into that game with contrasting club questions attached. Both still carry clear Chelsea relevance.

Sarr has not been the loudest Chelsea story of the tournament.

That may actually make this test more useful.

The 20-year-old is still moving through the awkward stage between prospect, squad option and saleable BlueCo asset.

Knockout football against Belgium can sharpen that picture quickly.

The timing is awkward in the best possible way for Chelsea. Alonso steps into a squad with expensive centre-backs, academy-trained options and a board still comfortable using the market aggressively.

A disciplined Sarr performance would not end that search. It would give the recruitment team a stronger internal benchmark before committing another major fee.

Chelsea need defenders who can hold a high line, cover wide channels and still pass through pressure. Belgium should ask those questions more directly than most group-stage opponents.

The context matters. Chelsea’s recall note recorded that Sarr returned from Strasbourg after 18 appearances across Ligue 1 and the Conference League.

The club also noted that he had already earned his first Senegal cap.

That is a different profile from an academy player being carried by reputation alone.

There is a statistical base behind the interest too. When Chelsea completed the deal, beIN SPORTS noted that Sarr made 27 Ligue 1 appearances in his first Strasbourg season.

He helped them keep 10 clean sheets. He also produced a team-high 20 blocks and made 25 interceptions.

Those numbers explain why this Belgium game is not just a sentimental World Cup subplot.

Alonso’s Chelsea defence is already crowded with Levi Colwill, Wesley Fofana, Trevoh Chalobah and external targets still orbiting the plan.

He is still being evaluated as a physical, long-range defensive project.

Jackson’s role changes the editorial weight of the tie.

Chelsea’s striker picture has been messy for long enough. Any high-pressure international performance now carries wider meaning.

ReadChelsea has already framed the forward’s tournament as a live Senegal striker audit for Chelsea.

Belgium should stress both Chelsea questions at once.

Jackson has to offer penalty-box threat and transition security. Sarr, if trusted, has to defend space against a technically cleaner opponent.

He also has to show whether his recovery pace and frame translate under tournament pressure.

Sarr’s own mentality profile is worth noting. In a Chelsea World Cup Q&A, he named Lionel Messi, Sadio Mane and Paul Pogba as his tournament heroes.

His answer on Pogba focused on leadership and group mentality.

That lands neatly with the exact question Chelsea now need answered. Is there enough presence to go with the physical tools?

This is why Belgium feels like a pathway check rather than a routine World Cup watch item.

Chelsea do not need Sarr to solve the defence in July. They need clearer evidence on whether he belongs in Alonso’s first pre-season group.

He could need another loan. He could also become part of the club’s centre-back market arithmetic.

For Jackson, the question is more immediate. For Sarr, it is more structural.

Together, Senegal’s knockout tie gives Chelsea a rare clean look at two players on opposite ends of the same squad-building argument.

Who can help now, and who is worth protecting for later?
